nodes.label: Catalyst Console
nodes.rationale: A driver station companion for FRC teams running FrcCatalyst. Tauri app: small Rust backend, plain HTML/CSS/JS frontend in the Windows WebView2. No framework, no bundler, no runtime network fetch; installer under four megabytes.

nodes.label: Rule 1 — It never controls the robot
nodes.rationale: FRC requires the official NI Driver Station and only one DS may hold the robot connection. The console does not open that socket and has no code path that could. Enable, disable and E-stop belong exclusively to the Driver Station.

nodes.label: Rule 2 — Nothing it does may impede driving
nodes.rationale: No modal blocks the dashboard, no check gates anything, no acknowledgement is ever required. Every failure degrades to a dimmed number and a quiet chip in the corner, so if the console breaks mid-match the driver keeps driving and need not notice.

nodes.label: Rule 3 — It never invents a number
nodes.rationale: A topic the robot has not published shows a dash, not a plausible value. The .dslog parser refuses versions it does not recognise rather than decoding them into nonsense. Demo data must be switched on deliberately and says so on screen while it runs.

nodes.label: NI Driver Station
nodes.rationale: The official FRC driver station. Only one may hold the robot connection, which is the whole basis of rule 1.

nodes.label: The second control path hazard
nodes.rationale: A tool that could drive would be a second control path to a robot, which is exactly what rule 1 forbids. Read-only is the design, not an unfinished feature.

nodes.label: The 10 Hz paint timer
nodes.rationale: The dashboard paints on a plain 10 Hz timer rather than only on requestAnimationFrame. Chromium stops firing animation frames for a window it considers occluded, so parking the Driver Station on top of an rAF-only dashboard would freeze it with stale numbers still on screen. This is rule 2 expressed as a repaint strategy.

nodes.label: Chromium stops rAF for an occluded window
nodes.rationale: The specific browser behaviour that makes an rAF-only dashboard unsafe on a driver station laptop, where the Driver Station window is routinely on top.

nodes.label: One console at a time
nodes.rationale: Launching again hands off to the running process, raises it and exits. Two consoles would mean two NetworkTables clients on one robot and a driver reading whichever happened to be on top.

nodes.label: The /FMSInfo write guard
nodes.rationale: All of /FMSInfo is read-only from the console's side, enforced in nt_set at the backend boundary rather than in the UI, so the guard holds whatever the frontend asks for.

nodes.label: /FMSInfo topics
nodes.rationale: Control word, alliance colour, event and match number, and the game-specific message. Carries no match time at all.

nodes.label: /FMSInfo/GameSpecificMessage
nodes.rationale: Names which alliance's hub goes inactive first. The hub schedule is derived from it plus the alliance colour.

nodes.label: Match clock topic fallback chain
nodes.rationale: /FMSInfo carries no time, so robot code must publish one. The console tries /Catalyst/Match/TimeLeft, then /SmartDashboard/MatchTime, then /FMSInfo/MatchTime, and takes the first that exists. With none of them the match timer and hub countdown show dashes rather than counting down from a number nobody published — rule 3 applied to the clock.

nodes.label: Hub activation tile
nodes.rationale: Answers one question from across the drive station: is our hub active, and how long until that changes. Colour carries it, countdown large underneath.

nodes.label: HUB versus TOWER terminology
nodes.rationale: The HUB is the fuel goal and the thing that goes active and inactive; the TOWER is the climbing structure in the alliance wall with its three rungs. Getting it backwards on a competition dashboard is not a harmless nickname.

nodes.label: REBUILT teleop shift schedule
nodes.rationale: Teleop runs 140 s in six segments (2026 Game Manual, Table 6-2). Transition shift and end game have both hubs active by rule; shifts 1-4 alternate, with the alliance that scored more fuel in auto inactive first.

nodes.label: Waiting for FMS game data rather than guessing
nodes.rationale: Before the game-specific message arrives the tile says so rather than guessing, because during shifts the answer genuinely depends on an auto result nothing else can infer. Rule 3 applied to the hub schedule.

nodes.label: A robot-published answer always wins
nodes.rationale: If the robot would rather compute the hub schedule itself, publish a boolean and a countdown and configure the tile to read them. The robot's own answer overrides the console's derivation.

nodes.label: The robot's spec sheet
nodes.rationale: A robot on FrcCatalyst 1.10+ publishes its own account of itself under /Catalyst/Robot/ — name, drivetrain geometry, mass, power, and the Catalyst features it runs. Drawn to scale from its own published figures.

nodes.label: RobotIdentity.declare
nodes.rationale: One line in RobotContainer is the whole adoption; everything else the library derives rather than accepting as input.

nodes.label: Absence rather than a dash on the spec sheet
nodes.rationale: A key the robot did not publish produces no row, and an empty group produces no group. A dash on a Gyro row would say this robot has no gyro; absence says it did not mention one, and only the second is true. The one place the console inverts its own dash convention, and still rule 3.

nodes.label: The Catalyst feature inventory
nodes.rationale: From 1.11 the sheet leads with which parts of the library the robot actually runs — Autopilot, Strategist, Sequence, Goal Director, Physics Core — each recorded by the component as it is built rather than declared anywhere. Two robots with the same drivetrain and motor count can still be completely different machines, and this is the only part of the sheet that says so.

nodes.label: Physics Core
nodes.rationale: Publishes pose, slip factor, tipping usage, traction usage and estimator confidence on its own once constructed. Slip, tipping and traction are all fraction-of-limit-in-use, so all three read the same way round: higher is worse.

nodes.label: Physics Core is advisory only
nodes.rationale: Physics Core has been validated in simulation and has never run on carpet; nothing on this dashboard should be gating a driver decision yet. The tile says advisory only on its face, deliberately.

nodes.label: The collision group and the Impacts tile
nodes.rationale: A new timestamp is what marks a new hit, rather than the same one still being reported.

nodes.label: The tunables manifest
nodes.rationale: The robot declares in one JSON string at /Catalyst/Tunables/.manifest what it is willing to let a dashboard change. The console shows what is in that list and nothing else — it never infers that a topic looks tunable, so a value you did not declare cannot be changed from here.

nodes.label: Demo data
nodes.rationale: Synthetic telemetry for a board with no robot. Exists, has to be switched on deliberately, and says so on screen while it runs — the concession rule 3 makes, fenced so it cannot be mistaken for a robot.

nodes.label: Driver Station logs
nodes.rationale: The .dsevents and .dslog files the NI DS already writes, parsed into a timeline. Some of that exists nowhere else: the robot never sees its own packet loss, because the packets that would have told it are the ones that went missing.

nodes.label: The .dslog parser fails closed
nodes.rationale: The formats are community-reverse-engineered rather than documented by NI, so a header the parser does not recognise is reported as unparsed and the event log is still shown. Inventing a battery voltage would be worse than admitting the file cannot be read.

nodes.label: The read-only diagnostics MCP server
nodes.rationale: The same binary run with --mcp opens no window and serves read-only diagnostics over stdio so an agent can see what the robot is doing. Read-only is the whole design: a tool that could drive would be a second control path.

nodes.label: Two modes, one binary
nodes.rationale: catalyst-console launches a dashboard window; catalyst-console --mcp serves diagnostics on stdio instead. --help explains both.

nodes.label: Strict CSP and vendored three.js
nodes.rationale: npm run vendor copies three.js into src/vendor/ and must run before the first build: the webview runs under script-src 'self', so nothing loads from a CDN. A dashboard that needs the internet to draw a field is a dashboard that fails in exactly the venue it is meant for.

nodes.label: The baked field model
nodes.rationale: The KOP CAD glTF is 223 MB and 6.8 million vertices — a fine marketing asset and a terrible dashboard one. npm run field-cad decimates it to about 190k vertices and 6 MB, a 36x reduction that still reads as the REBUILT field. Deliberately not committed: it is FIRST's model rather than ours.

nodes.label: The procedural field outline
nodes.rationale: With no baked model the view draws the field from its dimensions — carpet, perimeter, driver station glass, centre and alliance lines. Not a placeholder to apologise for: it is what renders on a machine that has never seen the CAD, and it is the version that always works.

nodes.label: Field material re-grounding
nodes.rationale: The KOP model is lit for a render, so its unpainted parts arrive near-white — a slab of glare in a dark cockpit that pulls your eye away from the robot. Each material keeps its hue so alliance red and blue still read, but saturation and lightness come right down and the field recedes behind the thing you are actually watching.

nodes.label: Field render cost control
nodes.rationale: Because this shares a laptop with the Driver Station: 30 fps, no shadows, no textures, no post-processing, ~30 meshes, rendering stops entirely when the dashboard tab is not showing, and three.js is only fetched when a field tile exists in the layout.

nodes.label: 20 Hz batched flush
nodes.rationale: nt4.rs batches values into a map and flushes on a fixed cadence rather than emitting at wire rate. The robot publishes at 50 Hz across hundreds of topics; pushing each change straight into the webview would spend the whole frame budget in IPC. UI cost is made independent of how chatty the robot is.

nodes.label: Layout export and import
nodes.rationale: Export the board as JSON and every laptop in the pit comes up the same.

nodes.label: A stored board that cannot be read does not take the console with it
nodes.rationale: Each tile is checked on the way out of storage and an unreadable one is dropped with a console warning — silence and nine of ten tiles beats a dialog and none. If building the board throws anyway the console falls back to its shipped layout. Not tidiness: the build runs at module scope, so a throw there used to abort the rest of the file, taking the repaint loop, the keyboard listener and the panel stand-down with it and leaving a driver an empty board that still looked healthy. Storage is left untouched, because the board that could not be built is still the board somebody arranged.

nodes.label: Candidate address cycling
nodes.rationale: The console cycles 127.0.0.1, roborio-TEAM-frc.local, 10.TE.AM.2 and 172.22.11.2 until one answers, so the same build works everywhere with no setting to forget.

nodes.label: The team number lives in the backend config
nodes.rationale: Kept by the backend in the app's own config directory rather than in the webview's storage, because --mcp has to read the same answer with no webview involved.

nodes.label: The Settings panel
nodes.rationale: One panel holding everything the console lets you change about itself, replacing a set of modals hanging off chips in the top strip, and About with them. A mode of the instrument rather than a window over it.

nodes.label: Settings stands down when the robot goes live
nodes.rationale: Nothing in the panel is modal, nothing has an apply button, and the whole panel stands down the instant the robot is enabled or E-stopped. That last part is rule two: whatever the console has to say about itself, none of it is worth reading over the top of a state lamp.

nodes.label: Settings search leaves matches where they live
nodes.rationale: Typing filters every row in every section at once and leaves each match where it lives, so a setting found by searching is changed the same way as one found by navigating — it is the same row, with the handler it was built with.

nodes.label: Units, metric or imperial
nodes.rationale: Changes how the spec sheet reads and nothing else; the robot always publishes SI and nothing on the wire moves. It exists because FRC writes its frame perimeter and height rules in inches, so a team checking legality is otherwise converting by hand at exactly the moment they cannot afford an arithmetic mistake.

nodes.label: Settings storage is validated key by key
nodes.rationale: A value out of range is pulled back into it and anything else falls back to the default, because a bad number out of storage lands in a component that has no business validating a setting.

nodes.label: Competition legality
nodes.rationale: It is a dashboard: it connects to NetworkTables and displays what it finds, as Shuffleboard, Glass, Elastic and AdvantageScope all do. It does not touch the DS protocol and does not open a second control connection. The team is responsible for checking the season manual.

nodes.label: FrcCatalyst
nodes.rationale: The robot-side library this console is a companion to. Versions 1.10+ publish the spec sheet, 1.11+ the feature inventory, 1.12+ the CAN device tree.

nodes.label: Alert group topics
nodes.rationale: Catalyst's AlertManager publishes string arrays at /Catalyst/Alerts/Errors, Warnings and Info; WPILib's own widget uses lowercase errors/warnings/infos. The tile reads whichever is present rather than making you pick, and the group path is configurable.

nodes.label: Auto chooser
nodes.rationale: Standard SendableChooser. The console reads options and selected under the chooser path and writes selected when you pick one — the same key Shuffleboard writes. One of only two things the console ever writes.

nodes.label: Shortest distinguishing path suffix
nodes.rationale: With several topics on one gauge, labels are derived from the shortest path suffix that actually distinguishes them — four keys ending in /Velocity come out as FrontLeft / FrontRight / BackLeft / BackRight rather than Velocity four times.

nodes.label: Trust the robot, not the dashboard
nodes.rationale: If something here disagrees with what your robot is actually doing, trust the robot — because a dashboard that is confidently wrong is worse than one that says it does not know. The three rules stated as a disposition rather than a mechanism.

nodes.label: Documentation index
nodes.rationale: The docs landing page: installing, settings, the garage, widgets, the hub schedule, the diagnostics MCP server, and the contract with the robot.

nodes.label: The three rules, restated in the docs index
nodes.rationale: A compressed restatement of the same three rules the README states in full, placed at the head of the documentation set so every page is read under them.
